lesson.title: Naming a Recipe: Why Functions Exist
lesson.summary: A function packages a sequence of steps under a single name, so a task you might otherwise repeat or reason through line by line can instead be built once and reused as a unit.
lesson.body:
Every program you write is ultimately a sequence of instructions, but as programs grow, keeping every instruction spelled out in one long block becomes unmanageable. This is the same challenge stepwise refinement addresses at the level of planning: instead of solving a big problem in one leap, you break it into smaller, named subtasks, and work out each one on its own. Functions are the concrete tool Python gives you to carry that decomposition into actual code. A function takes a sequence of statements that accomplish some task and gives that sequence a name, so the rest of your program can refer to the task by name instead of by its full list of steps.

This is abstraction in its most direct programming form. When you call a function like print() or len(), you do not think about how printing pushes characters onto a screen, or how len() walks through a sequence counting elements. You trust the name to represent the behavior, and you focus on what you need, not how it happens internally. Writing your own functions extends this same courtesy to your own code: once you define a function that checks whether a number is prime, every later part of your program can just say is_prime(17) and get an answer, without repeating the checking logic or forcing the reader to relearn how primality testing works every time it is used.

Functions solve a second, very practical problem: repetition. Suppose a program needs to compute the average of a list of numbers in three different places. Without functions, you would either copy and paste the averaging code three times, which means fixing a bug requires finding and correcting three separate copies, or you write it once as a function and call it three times, so a single fix in one place fixes every use. This is often summarized as "don't repeat yourself," and it is one of the strongest practical arguments for using functions even in fairly small programs.

Consider a tiny worked example that shows the shape of the idea, even though the exact syntax for defining a function is covered next. def greet(name): return "Hello, " + name + "!" creates a function named greet that takes one piece of information, name, and produces a greeting string built from it. Calling greet("Amara") runs the body with name bound to "Amara", and the return statement hands back "Hello, Amara!" as the result. Calling greet("Diego") reuses the exact same code with a different name bound in, producing "Hello, Diego!" instead. Nothing about the function itself changed between the two calls, only the specific value flowing through it did, which is the essence of what makes a function reusable rather than a one-off block of code glued to a single scenario.

Thinking in terms of functions also changes how you approach solving a problem in the first place. Rather than staring at an entire assignment and trying to write it top to bottom, you can ask what smaller, nameable subtasks the problem breaks into, sketch a function for each one, and worry about wiring them together only after each piece works on its own. That habit of decomposing before coding is exactly what stepwise refinement describes, and functions are what let that plan survive contact with real, running code.
